name: Auditorium Shores Off-Leash Area
metaTitle: Auditorium Shores Dog Park Austin | Free Off-Leash Area on Lady Bird Lake
metaDescription: Auditorium Shores is Austin's most scenic off-leash dog park — free access along Lady Bird Lake with downtown skyline views, swimming, and open grassy areas. Open daily 5am–10pm.
description:
Auditorium Shores Off-Leash Area is Austin's most iconic dog park — a wide, open stretch of Lady Bird Lake waterfront where dogs run free against a backdrop of the downtown skyline. The off-leash area sits along the south shore of Lady Bird Lake near Barton Springs Road, giving dogs direct access to the lake for swimming while owners enjoy one of the best views in the city. On any given morning or evening you'll find dozens of dogs ranging from golden retrievers to pit mixes charging the water, chasing balls across the grass, and socializing with the regular crowd that shows up here daily. The park is unfenced — this is important. Auditorium Shores is a wide open space, not an enclosed dog park, so dogs need solid recall before you bring them here. The lake access is shallow and gradual near the off-leash zone, making it manageable for most dogs that like water. Parking is available in the lot off W Riverside Drive, though it fills up fast on weekend mornings. The surrounding trail connects to the larger Lady Bird Lake hike and bike trail, so many owners combine a dog park visit with a longer walk. Hours are 5am to 10pm daily. No fees. Leashes required outside the designated off-leash area. Waste bags and stations are available on-site. The park can get crowded on weekend mornings — if you have a reactive dog or prefer a quieter environment, weekday early mornings are the best window. Located at 900 W Riverside Dr, Austin, TX 78704, just west of the Lamar Bridge.

Austin Parks and Recreation warns that toxic algae has been found in Lady Bird Lake and is most likely present in summer and autumn. It can be fatal to dogs, which are exposed both by drinking and by licking it off their coat afterwards. Avoid floating algae mats and scummy still water at the edges, and rinse your dog with clean water when you leave.
features: Water access to Lady Bird Lake

name: Bartholomew District Park
description:
Bartholomew District Park in East Austin has one of the few fully fenced off-leash dog parks on the east side of I-35, making it a convenient option for dog owners in the Mueller, Windsor Park, and Govalle neighborhoods. The park has separate sections for small and large dogs, which helps keep size-mismatched interactions to a minimum and gives smaller dogs a safe space to run without getting overwhelmed.

The fenced areas have a mix of grass and packed dirt, some shade trees, and water stations. The park isn't enormous, but for a neighborhood off-leash spot it's well-maintained and regularly used by a friendly, regular crowd. Weekend mornings tend to draw the biggest turnout — which is good for socialization but means the grass takes a beating during dry stretches.

Bartholomew is located off Berkman Drive in the 51st Street corridor, with a parking lot off the main park entrance. The broader Bartholomew District Park also has sports fields, picnic areas, and a pool — so it's a full-service park with the dog area as one component rather than the entire property.

The wider park is the reason to make it a longer stop. Bartholomew has a municipal pool, sports fields and picnic areas alongside the dog run, so the fenced area is one component of a full-service park rather than the whole destination — useful if someone in the group loses interest in watching dogs.

Be realistic about the surface. The enclosure sees heavy daily use from a dense catchment, and in a dry stretch the grass gives way to packed dirt and dust. It recovers after rain, but midsummer is not when this park looks its best.
features: Separate small and large dog areas
metaTitle: Bartholomew District Park Dog Park — Fenced Off-Leash in East Austin | ATX Dog Parks
metaDescription: Bartholomew District Park has a fenced off-leash dog park in East Austin with separate small and large dog sections. Near Mueller and Windsor Park. Free parking, water stations on site.

name: Barton Creek Greenbelt
address: 3755 S Capital of Texas Hwy, Austin, TX 78704
description:
The Barton Creek Greenbelt is one of Austin's most beloved outdoor spaces, and it's genuinely dog-friendly across its nearly 8 miles of trail — leashes are required, but the greenbelt's mix of shaded trails, limestone cliffs, and natural swimming holes makes it one of the best on-leash outings in the city. The creek runs through the entire length of the greenbelt, and multiple spots allow dogs to wade or swim depending on water levels.

There are several access points: Barton Springs Road (most popular, fills up fast), Loop 360 at Spyglass, Campbell's Hole, and the Twin Falls entrance. The terrain varies from flat, packed trail near the main entrances to rugged, rocky sections with creek crossings further in. Dogs should be comfortable on uneven terrain for the longer sections. The payoff is real — deep, clear pools surrounded by limestone canyon walls with tree cover that keeps temperatures tolerable even in summer.

Water levels vary dramatically with rainfall — after heavy rain, some sections can be inaccessible or unsafe. During dry summers, the swimming holes shrink but rarely disappear entirely. Weekends at the Barton Springs entrance are very crowded; the Twin Falls or Loop 360 entrances are better bets for a quieter hike. Bring water for both you and your dog on longer stretches since creek water quality varies. This is a go-to outing for Austin dog owners and worth the minor logistics.

The swimming holes are what people actually come for, and they are worth knowing by name. Campbell's Hole is closest to the Spyglass access and the easiest to reach with a dog. Gus Fruh has deeper water and a cliff wall that draws climbers. Twin Falls and Sculpture Falls sit further south and take a proper walk to reach, which is exactly why they are quieter.

How much water is in any of them depends entirely on recent rain. In a dry Austin summer the upper sections can run to standing pools or nothing at all, while the lower holes hold water most of the year. After a storm the creek moves fast enough through the narrow limestone sections to be genuinely dangerous for a dog.

Two cautions on the water itself. Austin has recurring problems with toxic algae in its waterways, which can kill dogs — keep them away from mats and scum on still water and rinse them off afterwards. And creek water quality here varies with runoff, so bring drinking water rather than letting your dog rely on the creek.

Footing is the other thing to plan for. Much of the greenbelt is loose limestone, exposed root and rock shelf rather than groomed trail. It rewards a sure-footed dog and punishes a clumsy one, and the same goes for whoever is holding the leash.
metaTitle: Barton Creek Greenbelt Austin — Dog-Friendly Hiking & Natural Swimming Holes | ATX Dog Parks
metaDescription: Barton Creek Greenbelt has 8 miles of dog-friendly trails with limestone swimming holes in central Austin. Leash required. Multiple access points. Best for active dogs who love water and trails.

name: Bob Wentz Park at Windy Point
hours: 8:00 AM - 8:00 PM Daily (no new entries after 7:30 PM)
fees: $5 per person day use; $3 seniors 62+; free 12 and under. Cash only.
description:
Bob Wentz Park is a Travis County park on the north shore of Lake Travis, and there are several things to sort out before you drive out, because a fair amount of what gets written about it online is wrong.

It is not free. Day use is $5 per person, $3 for seniors 62 and over, and no charge for children 12 and under or for disabled veterans at 50 percent or greater. **The entrance booth takes cash only** — no cards, no phones, no exceptions — and people do get turned around at the gate over this. If you end up coming often, the $80 Travis County resident annual permit covers day use here and at eight other county parks.

Dogs must be leashed everywhere in the park. Off-leash is explicitly prohibited, so despite the swimming this is a lake outing with your dog rather than a dog park in the usual sense.

The bigger catch is The Point. That small sandy peninsula with the covered picnic tables and the easiest water access is exactly where you would want to take a dog, and **pets are not allowed on it at all**. Plenty of visitors find this out after parking. There is still plenty of shoreline elsewhere in the 211 acres, but it is rockier limestone rather than sand, so bring something for your feet and expect a less gentle entry into the water.

Two water cautions that matter more for dogs than for people. The LCRA advises keeping dogs away from floating algae mats on the Highland Lakes and rinsing them with clean water after they swim — toxic algae has been a recurring problem on Austin waterways and it can be fatal to dogs that lick it off their coat. Zebra mussels have also been found along the shoreline, and their shells are sharp enough to cut paws in the shallows.

The park is a well-known windsurfing and sailing spot, which tells you what the conditions are like: it is genuinely windy most days and the surface gets choppy. That is fine for wading and shoreline fetch, less good for a dog inclined to strike out for the middle of the lake.

Hours are 8am to 8pm daily, and the gate stops admitting new entries thirty minutes before closing. On holiday weekends the park fills and then closes to all incoming traffic for the rest of the day, including people on foot, so an early start matters more here than at a city park. Drinking fountains, restrooms, showers and covered picnic tables are on site.

It is roughly a 30-minute drive from downtown, which along with the entry fee makes this a deliberate weekend trip rather than a stop on the way home.
features: Pets NOT allowed on The Point
Restrooms, showers and covered picnic tables
metaTitle: Bob Wentz Park at Windy Point — Dogs & Lake Travis Swimming in West Austin | ATX Dog Parks
metaDescription: Bob Wentz Park on Lake Travis offers stunning views and rocky shoreline swimming for dogs. West Austin near Comanche Trail. Dogs on-leash required. Day-use fee. Best weekend morning destination.

name: Bull Creek District Park
description:
Bull Creek District Park is one of the best places in Austin to be near water with a dog, and also one of the most misreported. It is worth getting the rules right before you go.

**This is an on-leash park.** Austin Parks and Recreation removed off-leash privileges here after fecal contamination was found in Bull Creek and off-leash dog use was identified as the likely source. Plenty of what is written about the park online still describes it as a place where the leash rule is loosely observed at the water. We would rather not point you at that: the restriction exists because of a water quality problem in a creek that feeds into Lake Austin, and the dogs standing in it are the reason. Check the posted signage when you arrive, since rules here have changed before and may change again.

None of which stops it being a lovely place to take a leashed dog. The limestone creek bed steps down through a series of shallow pools shaded by bluffs and mature trees, and it stays genuinely cool in the middle of a Texas summer when almost nothing else outdoors does. Wading in the shallows on a long lead is most of what people come for.

Two cautions on the water. Swimming areas at Bull Creek have been closed at times over blue-green algae, which is toxic to dogs and can kill them — avoid still water with mats or scum on the surface, and rinse your dog afterwards. And the level swings hard with rainfall: after a dry spell the pools shrink to ankle depth, while after a storm the current through the rock channels is stronger than it looks.

The footing is rough. This is a natural creek bed, not a groomed park — loose limestone, uneven slabs, and slick rock under the water. Dogs with joint problems or poor balance will find it hard work, and so will you in the wrong shoes.

Access is off Lakewood Drive, just south of Loop 360. Parking is free but the lot is small and fills early on any decent weekend; before 9am or after 4pm gives you a realistic chance.
features: Limestone creek beds and shallow pools
Deep shade from bluffs and mature trees
metaTitle: Bull Creek District Park Austin — Dog Swimming in Natural Limestone Creek | ATX Dog Parks
metaDescription: Bull Creek is Austin's best natural dog swimming spot — limestone creek pools stay cool through summer. NW Austin near Loop 360. Rocky terrain, leash required on trails.

name: Cedar Bark Park
address: 2525 W New Hope Dr, Cedar Park, TX 78613
hours: 6:00 AM - 10:00 PM (Tue opens 3:00 PM, Fri opens 11:00 AM for maintenance)
description:
Cedar Bark Park is five fenced acres inside Veterans Memorial Park on West New Hope Drive. It is not at Elizabeth Milburn Park, which is a separate Cedar Park facility a few miles away and a common mix-up.

The draw here is water. There's a dog pond for swimming and, more unusually, dog showers on site — so the muddy retriever who just discovered the pond doesn't have to ride home that way. Drinking fountains, waste stations, and benches are spread through the grounds, and the site keeps a fair amount of natural landscape rather than being scraped flat and sodded.

Check the day before you drive over, because the maintenance schedule closes the park on two mornings a week. Tuesdays it stays shut from 7am until 3pm, and Fridays from 7am until 11am, while the city services the wash stations and clears trash. Every other day runs 6am to 10pm.

Cedar Park asks visitors to be diligent about picking up, and the reason is specific rather than generic: waste left near the pond ends up in the water the dogs are swimming in.

The pond is a genuine one rather than a splash pad — a fenced basin with an aerating fountain in the middle and a short dock along one edge. The bank is gravel with a concrete ramp giving dogs a gradual way in and out instead of a drop, and on a warm afternoon there are usually a few standing in the shallows near the ramp rather than swimming properly.

Entry is through a double gate, and the small and large sides are split at 30 pounds. In the large field there is a dachshund-shaped tunnel that puppies find considerably more interesting than the adult dogs do.
metaTitle: Cedar Bark Park | 5-Acre Dog Park with Pond & Showers in Cedar Park
metaDescription: Cedar Park's 5-acre fenced dog park in Veterans Memorial Park, with a swimming pond and dog wash stations. Closed Tuesday mornings and Friday mornings for maintenance. Free.

name: Dog Depot Dog Park
hours: 6:00 AM - 8:00 PM (Apr 1 - Oct 1); 6:00 AM - 6:00 PM (Oct 2 - Mar 31)
description:
Round Rock's off-leash park is Dog Depot, 1.85 fenced acres behind the Lake Creek Pool on Deerfoot Drive. Worth stating up front, because it trips people up: this is not at Old Settlers Park. Old Settlers is the bigger name in town and the one people assume, but dogs there are leash-only.

The layout is unusual in a way that pays off. There are three sections instead of the usual two — a large dog area, a small dog area for anything under 40 pounds, and a rotation area the city closes off periodically so the grass can recover. That third section is why the footing here holds up better than at most parks getting this much traffic.

The gates are winding sally-port entrances, which makes it much harder for a dog to slip past you on the way in or out. Agility equipment is spread through the large side: a tire jump, an A-frame contact ramp, and a tunnel.

Two rules catch visitors off guard. No food of any kind is allowed inside, and that includes training treats. And every dog must be both vaccinated and microchipped — Round Rock states it directly rather than burying it in fine print.

Hours shift seasonally: 6am to 8pm from April 1 through October 1, then 6am to 6pm from October 2 through March 31. Restrooms are at the Lake Creek Park pavilion outside the fence, in front of the pool, and there are hand sanitizer stations at the gates.

The no-food rule deserves emphasis because it catches out anyone who trains with treats as a matter of routine. Round Rock means all food, not just meals, and the reasoning is straightforward: food in a shared enclosure is the most reliable way to start a fight between dogs that were getting along fine.
features: Large dog, small dog (under 40 lbs) and rotation areas
Agility equipment: tire jump, A-frame ramp, tunnel
Restrooms at Lake Creek Park pavilion
No food or treats permitted inside
metaTitle: Dog Depot Dog Park Round Rock | 1.85-Acre Off-Leash Park on Deerfoot Dr
metaDescription: Round Rock's off-leash dog park: 1.85 fenced acres behind Lake Creek Pool with separate large, small and rotation areas, agility equipment and sally-port gates. Microchip required. Free.

name: Dog House Drinkery & Dog Park
hours: Mon Closed; Tue-Thu 3:00 PM - 9:00 PM; Fri 3:00 PM - 10:00 PM; Sat 12:00 PM - 10:00 PM; Sun 12:00 PM - 9:00 PM
fees: $8 day pass, $200/year membership (+$50 per additional dog)
description:
Central Texas' original off-leash dog park bar, running since 2013 — Dog House Drinkery sits in Leander, about 25 minutes north of downtown Austin, not in South Austin as its name might suggest to anyone going off memory. The dog area is a fenced half-acre yard with park monitors on duty, attached to a full bar with beer, wine, and seltzers plus shaded patio seating.

It's closed Mondays (aside from occasional special events), then open Tuesday through Sunday with a $8 day pass or a $200 annual membership that covers one dog (additional dogs are $50/year each). Bring a copy of your dog's vaccination records — digital, tag, or paper all work, but they check.

The crowd draws from Leander, Cedar Park, Round Rock, and Liberty Hill as much as Austin proper, so plan on the drive if you're coming from central or south Austin.

A few rules catch people out. **The main park is 16 and over** — it is a bar with a dog yard attached, not a family venue, and the private event space is the part that accommodates younger visitors. Dogs must be spayed or neutered. Outside food is not allowed in the main yard, though food trucks turn up some evenings and there is a full bar inside.

The referees are the real differentiator versus a public park. Staff are in the yard watching play rather than sitting behind a counter, and they will step in on a dog that is being a problem long before the owners would. If you have been put off public runs by unsupervised dogs, that supervision is most of what the entry fee buys.

Beyond the yard there is indoor and outdoor dog-friendly seating, big-screen TVs, foosball and cornhole, so it functions as somewhere to spend an evening rather than a twenty-minute stop. Worth doing the arithmetic on the pass, though: at $8 a visit, anyone going weekly is better off on the $200 annual membership within about six months.
features: Full bar with beer, wine, and seltzers
No outside food in main yard
Indoor seating, TVs, foosball and cornhole
metaTitle: Dog House Drinkery & Dog Park — Leander's Off-Leash Bar | ATX Dog Parks
metaDescription: Dog House Drinkery & Dog Park in Leander is Central Texas' original off-leash dog park bar — fenced half-acre yard, full bar, open Tue-Sun. $8 day pass or annual membership.

name: Domain Central Dog Park
metaTitle: Domain Central Dog Park Austin — Fenced Off-Leash at The Domain | ATX Dog Parks
metaDescription: Domain Central Dog Park is a free, fenced off-leash park inside The Domain in North Austin. Separate small/large dog areas, mature shade, double-gate entry. Park then shop or dine nearby.
description:
Domain Central Dog Park sits inside the Domain retail district in north Austin, off Alterra Parkway near the H-E-B. It is fully fenced with double-gated entry and separate large and small sides, which makes it one of the more forgiving places in north Austin to work with a dog that is not yet reliable off-leash.

The park is not big. Mature trees give it decent shade and the grass holds up better than most heavily used city runs, because it is maintained by the property rather than the city — but at 5pm on a weekday, or on a Saturday morning, it fills, and a small fenced space with a lot of dogs in it is a different proposition from the same space at ten on a Tuesday. If your dog finds crowding stressful, the timing matters more here than the facilities do.

What it has over almost every other option in north Austin is that it is embedded in somewhere you were probably going anyway. You can run the dog for half an hour and then do the grocery shop, or eat, without a second trip. Parking is in the Domain garages and the first two hours are free, which covers a normal visit comfortably.

The mixed crowd is worth flagging. Because the district draws people from across the city rather than one neighborhood, you get more first-time visitors and fewer regulars who know each other's dogs than you would at a place like Hancock or West Austin. That cuts both ways — friendlier to a newcomer, less predictable in terms of who is watching their dog.

name: Emma Long Metropolitan Park
leashPolicy: On-Leash on trails, Off-leash in designated areas
fees: $5 per vehicle Mon-Thu; $10 Fri-Sun and holidays. Turkey Creek Trail lot is before the pay station and free.
description:
Emma Long is Austin's largest city park at 1,147 acres, running along the south shore of Lake Austin, and it is genuinely rugged — narrow winding access road, uneven ground, hill country terrain that feels a long way from town despite being inside the city limits.

**Get the fees right before you go, because ours were wrong until recently and most listings still are.** Entry is **$5 Monday through Thursday and $10 Friday through Sunday and on holidays**, per vehicle. It is not free on weekdays.

**There is a way around the fee if the off-leash area is your destination.** The leash-free area sits between City Park Road, the western boundary fence, Turkey Creek and the ridge above Lake Austin, and it is reached from the Turkey Creek Trail — where the parking lot sits *before* the pay station. Park there and the trail costs nothing.

One honest caveat on that off-leash status. The city's trail directory lists Turkey Creek with an off-leash designation, while the park rules page states that pets must remain leashed and under control at all times. Those two city sources genuinely contradict each other. We are not going to tell you which to believe — check posted signage when you arrive, and if in doubt, a leash costs you nothing.

Turkey Creek Trail itself is the main draw regardless: a shaded loop of roughly two and a half miles with repeated creek crossings, which makes it one of the better summer walks in Austin for a dog that likes water.

Down in the main park there are several points of Lake Austin frontage where dogs can swim, plus primitive and improved camping, picnic areas and restrooms. Austin's guidance on toxic algae in local waterways applies here too — avoid still water with surface mats, and rinse your dog afterwards.

Hours are 7am to 10pm. The road in from FM 2222 is narrow, winding and slow; allow more time than the distance suggests.
features: Turkey Creek Trail (~2.5 mi, shaded, creek crossings)
Free parking at the Turkey Creek lot, before the pay station
Off-leash status disputed between city sources - check signage
metaTitle: Emma Long Metropolitan Park Austin — Dogs, Trails & Lake Austin Swimming | ATX Dog Parks
metaDescription: Austin's largest city park — 1,147 acres with Lake Austin access and off-leash areas. Remote location off FM 2222. $5 entry. Great for adventurous dogs who want to swim and explore.

name: Falcon Pointe Garden and Bark Park
description:
Falcon Pointe's bark park is attached to a demonstration garden, which makes it the odd one out among Pflugerville's off-leash options and the more interesting place to spend an hour.

The dog side is 2.65 fenced acres split into separate large and small runs, each with its own gate off a shared concrete apron. Both gates have a waste bag dispenser and there's a water bowl set out between them. Note that the signs are pictures rather than a posted weight limit — a labrador silhouette on one gate, a corgi on the other — so unlike Cedar Bark, where the split is written as 30 pounds, sorting a borderline dog is left to your judgment.

The large run is genuinely large, closer to a field than a pen, with real turf rather than the worn dirt a lot of heavily used runs turn into. The ground near the gates is bare and packed from traffic, but it opens up quickly. Mature live oaks along the fence line give proper shade over a decent share of the space, and there are more young trees planted through the middle that will matter in another ten years. A soccer pitch sits immediately beyond the far fence, so on league mornings there's noise and movement on the other side of the rail — which matters if your dog fixates on that sort of thing.

What surrounds it is the unusual part. The grounds hold a village of purple martin houses, pear trees, and a set of themed demonstration gardens: rain, culinary, medicinal, butterfly and hummingbird, and native plantings. There's also a moon garden planted for evening visits, built around fragrant white flowers that show up after dark. If you walk your dog at dusk in summer because the afternoon is unbearable, that's more useful than it sounds.

The pavilion is the other landmark — a hexagonal shelter with a deep red roof and picnic tables, set on a concrete circle next to a repurposed grain silo. It's the obvious place to wait out a squall or eat something while the dog runs.

Open 6am to 10pm, free, with free parking. It sits off Murchison Ridge Trail on Pflugerville's east side. The field is open enough that there's little shelter from wind in winter, and the photographs of it under ice are a reminder that Central Texas does occasionally deliver that.
features: Separate large and small dog runs
Waste stations and water bowl at the gates
Demonstration gardens including a moon garden
metaTitle: Falcon Pointe Bark Park Pflugerville | Fenced Dog Park & Demonstration Gardens
metaDescription: Pflugerville's Falcon Pointe bark park: 2.65 fenced acres with separate small and large dog areas, boulder seating, purple martin houses and themed gardens. Open 6am-10pm. Free.

name: Garey Park
leashPolicy: On-Leash Required on Trails; Off-Leash Area Available
fees: $5/vehicle resident, $10/vehicle non-resident (up to 2 people); free Tuesdays Oct-Mar
description:
Garey Park's off-leash area is called the Dog Ranch, and it earns the name. Over four fenced acres of natural terrain rather than mown turf — brush, uneven ground, real cover — with separate enclosures for small and large dogs. For a dog that finds flat rectangles boring, this is a different kind of outing.

Five shaded picnic shelters sit inside the fence, with water stations and dog-height drinking fountains. The shelters matter more here than at a neighborhood park, because most people stay longer than the usual twenty minutes.

The Dog Ranch is one piece of a 525-acre former ranch on the South San Gabriel River, donated to Georgetown and opened to the public. Trails run down toward the water, there's fishing when the river is up, and 4.68 miles of equestrian trail if you ride. It sits about 6.5 miles west of I-35 on RM 2243.

Two things separate it from everything else in this directory. It charges admission, and the fee is per vehicle rather than per person: $5 for Georgetown residents and $10 for non-residents, covering a driver and one passenger, with each additional person $2. Annual passes run $100 resident and $150 non-resident. And from October through March, entry is free on Tuesdays — the cheapest way to see whether the drive is worth it.

Hours shift with the season: 8am to 8pm from April through September, 8am to 6pm from October through March. Nobody is admitted within 30 minutes of closing, and the park shuts on Thanksgiving, Christmas Eve and Christmas Day.

Worth understanding what you are paying for, because Garey is not a drop-in neighborhood run. The entry fee, the drive and the seasonal hours all point the same way: this is a half-day out rather than a twenty-minute leg-stretch. The Dog Ranch is the anchor, but the wider 525 acres — river frontage on the South San Gabriel, trails, an equestrian area and a playground — are what justify the trip.
features: Over 4 fenced acres of natural terrain
Separate small and large dog areas
5 shaded picnic shelters inside the fence
metaTitle: Garey Park Dog Ranch Georgetown | 4-Acre Off-Leash Park on the San Gabriel
metaDescription: The Dog Ranch at Garey Park: 4+ fenced acres of natural terrain, separate small and large dog areas, 5 shaded shelters. $5/vehicle resident, $10 non-resident. Free Tuesdays Oct-Mar.

name: Georgetown Bark Park
description:
Georgetown's Bark Park sits in a pecan grove on East Morrow Street, and the trees are the whole reason to choose it over a newer park. Most dog parks in the region are open turf with a couple of young shade structures. This one has mature canopy, which changes what an August afternoon feels like for everyone standing in it.

There are two fenced sections, split at 30 pounds — worth noting if your dog sits near the line, since other parks in the area draw it at 40. Both sides have drinking fountains for dogs and people, benches, trash cans, Mutt Mitt dispensers, and posted rules. There's an agility course on site for dogs that want something to do beyond laps.

Gates open at 5am and close at 10pm, an hour earlier on the front end than most Williamson County parks. Parking is on site. For maintenance issues or questions, Georgetown Parks and Recreation takes calls at 512-930-3595.

Georgetown is roughly 30 minutes north of central Austin, so this is a destination park for most Austin residents and a neighborhood one for anyone in Williamson County. The pecan shade makes the drive more defensible in summer than it would be otherwise.

The 30-pound line is worth flagging because it is not the regional standard. Cedar Bark uses the same threshold, but several other parks in the area either draw it at 40 or, like Falcon Pointe, post pictures and leave the judgment to you. A 35-pound dog is a large dog here and a small dog elsewhere.

Shade aside, the other thing this park does well is space per dog. It rarely reaches the density of the central Austin runs, so dogs that find crowding stressful tend to do better here even accounting for the drive.
features: Separate large and small dog areas (30 lb split)
Drinking fountains for dogs and people in both areas
metaTitle: Georgetown Bark Park | Shaded Off-Leash Dog Park in a Pecan Grove
metaDescription: Georgetown's free off-leash dog park on E Morrow St, set in a mature pecan grove. Separate large and small dog areas (30 lb split), agility course, water fountains. Open 5am-10pm.

name: Great Northern Dog Park
description:
Great Northern Dog Park is a fenced off-leash area in Allandale, tucked behind the houses off Great Northern Boulevard in north-central Austin. Its formal name on city documents is the Great Northern Detention Basin Off-Leash Area, and that is not just bureaucratic phrasing — the park is a stormwater detention basin that doubles as a dog park, which explains almost everything about the way it looks and behaves.

The practical consequence is space. This is a wide, open, grassy bowl rather than a small pen, with walking paths around it, so dogs get room to actually run rather than circle. It also means the ground is engineered to hold water, so after heavy rain sections of it are genuinely soggy and the low ground near the pond stays wet longer than you would expect.

Be realistic about what is not here. There are no drinking fountains, so bring water for your dog and yourself, and there is little in the way of shaded seating — the tree cover around the edges is thin and the middle is fully exposed. From June through September that combination makes this an early morning or evening park rather than a midday one. Waste bag stations are provided, and parking is free with wheelchair accessible entrances.

The retention pond is a feature people either like or avoid. Dogs will go in it. It is stormwater rather than a spring-fed creek, so what is in it depends on what has washed off the surrounding streets recently, and it is not somewhere to let a dog drink.

The crowd is a neighborhood one drawn from Allandale and Crestview rather than across the city, which keeps it calmer than the destination parks. For anyone in north-central Austin it is a reasonable everyday option, provided you bring your own water and pick your hour in summer.

The signage at the entrance tells you something about how the site works. Alongside the off-leash area sign there is a notice pointing out that dog waste is a leading water-quality and flood concern — not generic park boilerplate here, but the direct consequence of the ground being a stormwater basin. What is left on the grass goes into the pond and then into the drainage system.
metaTitle: Great Northern Dog Park Austin — Off-Leash Near North Loop & Rundberg | ATX Dog Parks
metaDescription: Great Northern Dog Park is a free, fenced off-leash park in North Austin near the North Loop area. Neighborhood feel, regular crowd, grassy open space. Good for daily off-leash runs.

name: Hancock Dog Park
description:
Hancock Dog Park is a small fenced run in central Austin, tucked off Kim Lane between Hyde Park and the Hancock golf course. It is not a destination park and does not pretend to be — the appeal is that it exists within a few minutes of a dense, walkable part of town where the alternative is driving to Bartholomew or further.

**One thing to check before you go: the hours are 8am to 8pm.** Most Austin parks run 5am to 10pm, and a fair number of people turn up here at seven in the morning out of habit and find it shut. In summer, when the sensible window for a dark-coated dog is before eight anyway, that restriction genuinely limits the park's usefulness.

The ground is a mix of grass and rock, and the rocky sections are more prominent than at most city runs — worth a thought for a dog with soft pads or one that skids into turns at speed. Mature trees give reasonable shade over part of the space, and there's seating.

Waste bags are provided. Water is less dependable: there is a fountain, but reports of it being off or dry are common enough that bringing your own is the safer assumption between May and September.

The crowd is a neighborhood one, largely the same faces on weekday mornings and weekend afternoons, and it is small enough that a single boisterous dog changes the character of the whole park for the duration. Parking is on the surrounding residential streets rather than a lot, which is straightforward on a weekday and less so on a weekend afternoon.
metaTitle: Hancock Dog Park Austin — Fenced Off-Leash Near Hyde Park | ATX Dog Parks
metaDescription: Hancock Dog Park is a free, fenced off-leash park in Central Austin near Hyde Park. Separate small/large dog areas. No frills, neighborhood feel. Easy street parking off 41st Street.

name: Harris Branch Dog Park
description:
Harris Branch Dog Park is a small neighborhood run in the Harris Branch development in north-east Austin, off Harris Branch Parkway. It is fenced, with separate large and small dog sides connected within the same enclosure, double-gated entry, agility obstacles, benches and water.

It is worth setting expectations honestly: this is a pocket park serving the surrounding subdivision, not a destination. Public ratings for it are noticeably lower than for the other fenced parks in this part of the city, and the recurring theme in reviews is size — the small-dog side in particular is compact, and on a busy evening the whole park can feel tight. If you have a dog that needs distance from others to stay comfortable, Northtown up the road is the roomier option.

What it does offer is proximity. For anyone living in Harris Branch, Pioneer Crossing or the surrounding 78754 streets, this is a walk rather than a drive, and a fenced space five minutes from home gets used far more often than a better park twenty minutes away. Shade comes from young trees around the perimeter, so it is thinner than at the older parks and the middle is exposed in summer.

Waste stations are provided and the grounds are generally kept clean. Parking is on the street alongside the park.

Check current hours and any posted rules on arrival — this is a neighborhood facility and signage on site is the reliable source.
features: Separate large and small dog sides
metaTitle: Harris Branch Dog Park — Small Fenced Off-Leash Park in North-East Austin
metaDescription: Fenced neighbourhood dog park on Harris Branch Pkwy in 78754, with separate large and small sides, agility obstacles and water. Compact - see how it compares to Northtown.

name: Historic Stagecoach Park Dog Park
address: 405 E. Loop St, Building 100, Buda, TX 78610
description:
Buda's off-leash dog park relocated here from the old Sportsplex site in January 2026, after the city closed that location in August 2025 to build out the new grounds on the east side of Historic Stagecoach Park. It's a straightforward setup: a small-dog yard for dogs under 30 pounds and a separate large-dog yard, both fenced, with a water source and benches and picnic tables for owners.

Hours shift with daylight — 6am to 9pm from March through September, 6am to 7pm the rest of the year. Because it shares the grounds with Stagecoach Park's pavilion, amphitheater, playground, and trail system, it's easy to turn a dog park stop into a longer outing if the weather's decent.

Worth knowing if you used the old Sportsplex location: that dog park is gone, not just renamed. This is a new build in a different part of town, on the east side of the historic park property off Main Street.

The shared grounds are the argument for coming here over a standalone run. The dog yards sit on the same property as Stagecoach Park's pavilion, amphitheater, playground and trail network, so a dog park visit folds into a longer outing without a second drive — genuinely useful if you have children who lose interest in watching dogs after fifteen minutes.

It is also worth checking the season before you go. The winter closing time of 7pm means that from October the park shuts before most people finish work, which makes it a weekend option for much of the year.
features: Shares grounds with Stagecoach Park trails and pavilion
metaTitle: Historic Stagecoach Park Dog Park — Buda's Off-Leash Park | ATX Dog Parks
metaDescription: Buda's off-leash dog park moved to Historic Stagecoach Park in January 2026, with separate small- and large-dog yards. Free, seasonal hours, water access, benches.

name: Mary Moore Searight Metropolitan Park
description:
Mary Moore Searight is one of the few Austin parks with a dedicated off-leash trail rather than a fenced pen. The loop runs a little over a mile through the north end of the park, on natural surface through cedar scrub and live oak, with a shallow creek crossing partway round that most dogs will stand in rather than swim.

The off-leash section is reached from 1st Street, south of Slaughter Lane. That matters, because navigating to the park's main Slaughter Lane address puts you at a different entrance with a fair walk to the dog trail.

The loop is marked but not fenced. Dogs need to be under voice control, and the trail has enough tree cover and bends that a dog fifty yards ahead is genuinely out of sight. The upside of the same feature is that this doesn't have the penned-in intensity of a small fenced run — dogs walk rather than mill around, which suits a lot of dogs better than a crowded enclosure does.

It's noticeably quieter than the central Austin parks. If your dog gets overwhelmed in a pack, or you'd rather not spend the visit managing introductions, the difference in atmosphere here is the main reason to make the drive south.

There's no water at the off-leash trailhead, so bring your own — the creek is not a drinking source, particularly after rain moves street runoff through it. Parking at the trailhead is free and rarely full, even at weekends.

Beyond the dog loop the park has miles of additional on-leash trail, a disc golf course and sports fields, so it's easy to extend the visit. Summer afternoons the shaded stretches of the loop do real work, but the open sections are exposed; mornings are the sensible window from June through September.
features: Off-leash loop trail, a little over a mile
metaTitle: Mary Moore Searight Metropolitan Park — Off-Leash Loop Trail South Austin | ATX Dog Parks
metaDescription: Mary Moore Searight has a 1-mile off-leash loop trail with creek access in South Austin near Slaughter Lane. Less crowded than central parks. Dogs need reliable recall — unfenced.

name: Northtown Dog Park
hours: 7:00 AM - 9:00 PM Daily (closed weekends following rain)
description:
Northtown Dog Park sits inside the larger Northtown park complex on Harris Ridge Boulevard in Pflugerville, alongside a disc golf course, adult and children's soccer fields, volleyball and a pecan grove. It is run by the Northtown Municipal Utility District rather than a city parks department, so questions, closures and maintenance go to the MUD on (512) 716-0759 or manager@northtownmud.org — not to Pflugerville or Austin Parks and Recreation.

You will see this park listed elsewhere as "Harris Ridge Dog Park," sometimes at 14400 rather than 14401. It is the same place. The MUD's own signage says Northtown.

The large and small sides are separately gated and clearly signed, each entered through its own gate off a concrete apron. Much of the ground is artificial turf, which is the detail that most sets this apart from other parks in the area: it drains, it does not turn to mud, and it stays usable through a wet spell when a grass run would be churned up. Other sections are natural grass and packed dirt, so you get both surfaces in one visit. Shade sails cover part of the turf, and mature trees do the rest along the fence lines.

There is agility equipment — ramps and similar — set out on the natural-surface section, along with tables, chairs and dog drinking fountains.

**One rule that catches people out: anything left behind gets thrown out.** Posted signage states that all items left in the park, toys and water bowls included, are disposed of daily. If you bring a favorite ball, take it home with you.

Hours are 7am to 9pm daily, and the park closes on weekends following rain to protect the natural-grass areas. It generally reopens once things dry out, but if it rained on a Friday night, check before loading the dog into the car on Saturday morning.

House rules are stricter than a typical city park: no alcohol, no glass containers, no motorized vehicles.

It sits just off I-35 near the Pflugerville and north Austin line, which makes it a practical stop for anyone commuting that corridor.
features: Separate large and small dog areas
Items left behind are removed daily
Inside the Northtown complex (disc golf, soccer, volleyball)
metaTitle: Northtown Dog Park (formerly listed as Harris Ridge) — Pflugerville Off-Leash Park
metaDescription: Fenced off-leash dog park on Harris Ridge Blvd in Pflugerville, run by Northtown MUD. Separate large and small sides, agility equipment, shade. Open 7am-9pm; closed weekends after rain.

name: Norwood Estate Dog Park
metaTitle: Norwood Estate Dog Park — Free Off-Leash Park in South Austin | ATX Dog Parks
metaDescription: Norwood Estate Dog Park on Edgecliff Terrace has separate areas for small and large dogs, water fountains, benches, and waste stations. Free, open 5am–10pm daily in South Austin.
description:
Norwood Estate sits on a bluff above Lady Bird Lake at the end of Edgecliff Terrace, and the thing regulars mention first is the shade. That is not a small detail in Austin. A good share of the city's fenced runs are open ground that turns punishing by ten in the morning from May through September, and the difference between a treed park and a bare one is the difference between a real visit and one lap of the fence before everyone gives up and goes home.

The park is fully fenced, which puts it in the minority here — many of Austin's off-leash options are open greenbelt or unfenced lakefront where solid recall is the price of entry. Norwood has a double-gated entry and a genuinely separate small-dog section, not a token corner, so a nervous ten-pounder does not have to negotiate with a pack of labradors. Water, benches and waste stations are on site, and the ground is packed dirt and tree roots rather than turf, which drains quickly but does turn to mud for a day or so after heavy rain.

Parking is free and immediately adjacent, which sounds mundane until you have circled Clarksville or Zilker for twenty minutes. On weekdays you will not think about it. Late weekend afternoons it fills.

Worth being straight about the crowd, because it is the main reason people either make this their regular park or quietly stop coming: supervision here runs uneven. This is a busy park in a dense part of town, and on a given evening you may find several dogs whose owners are at the far end on their phones. That is true of urban dog parks generally, but it comes up about Norwood more than most. If your dog is reactive, or small enough to get bowled over by accident, mornings are noticeably calmer and the small-dog side is a real separation rather than a nominal one.

The name comes from the Norwood House, the 1920s estate on the bluff above the park that has been under a long slow restoration. It is not part of the dog park and you cannot walk through it, but it explains the odd tucked-away approach — you turn off Riverside, the road narrows and drops, and it stops feeling like you are four minutes from downtown.
features: Separate areas for small and large dogs

name: Onion Creek District Park
metaTitle: Onion Creek District Park Dog Park (Dog Park Blue) — Off-Leash & Swimming | ATX Dog Parks
metaDescription: Dog Park Blue at Onion Creek District Park is one of South Austin's best off-leash areas with Onion Creek swimming access. 517 acres, unfenced. Dogs need solid recall. Free parking off Slaughter Ln.
description:
Onion Creek District Park covers 517 acres in South Austin, and the off-leash section within it is called Dog Park Blue — an unfenced area at the northeast tip of the park, close enough to Onion Creek that most dogs end up in the water within a few minutes of arriving.

The creek is the reason people come. It runs wide and shallow across most of this stretch, with gradual gravel banks rather than steep drops, which makes it approachable for dogs that are curious about water without being strong swimmers. In summer it is the difference between a walk and a genuinely cooling outing. Depth changes with recent rain, and after a real storm the current is stronger than it looks.

Because the area is unfenced, this is a park for dogs that come back when called. It is large, the wooded sections along the creek break sight lines quickly, and a dog that decides to follow an interesting smell can be out of view faster than you expect. Regulars here tend to be experienced off-leash owners and the culture reflects that. If your dog is still learning recall, one of the fenced options — Bartholomew, Domain Central, Cedar Bark — is a better place to build the skill first.

There are no water fountains at the off-leash section. Bring your own, particularly between May and September — the creek is not something you want your dog relying on for drinking water, especially after rain washes street runoff into it. Waste bag dispensers are distributed along the trails and are usually stocked.

Parking is free and there is normally room, with peak weekend mornings in good weather being the exception. The wider park has picnic facilities and additional trails if you want to extend the visit beyond the dog area.

Shade is patchy. Sections along the creek are well covered, but the open ground between the parking and the water is exposed, and in July and August the walk in is the hottest part of the trip. Early morning is the sensible window in summer; spring and autumn it is pleasant most of the day.

name: Red Bud Isle
description:
Red Bud Isle is a narrow peninsula jutting into Lake Austin near Tarrytown — and it's one of the best off-leash spots in the city for dogs who love water. There's no fence, so recall is important, but for dogs that are reliable off-leash this place is hard to beat. Multiple creek and lake access points let dogs wade in or swim depending on water levels, and the wooded trails through cedar and oak keep things shaded even on hot Austin days.

The entrance is off Redbud Trail just west of MoPac — look for the small parking area near the trailhead. Parking is free but the lot fills up fast on weekends and after work hours. Most regulars come early morning or on weekday afternoons to avoid the crowds. The trails are narrow and winding in spots, so larger packs of dogs can get a little chaotic at peak times.

Bring water for your dog — there are no water stations on the peninsula itself. The terrain is uneven in places with exposed roots and limestone rock, so dogs with mobility issues may have trouble on some sections. Overall it's a natural, low-infrastructure experience: no lights, no facilities, no benches — just trees, water, and trail. For water-loving dogs in central Austin, it doesn't get much better.

Austin Parks and Recreation warns that toxic algae has been found in Lady Bird Lake and is most likely present in summer and autumn. It can be fatal to dogs, which are exposed both by drinking and by licking it off their coat afterwards. Avoid floating algae mats and scummy still water at the edges, and rinse your dog with clean water when you leave.
features: Surrounded by water on three sides
metaTitle: Red Bud Isle Dog Park Austin — Off-Leash on Lake Austin Peninsula | ATX Dog Parks
metaDescription: Red Bud Isle is Austin's top off-leash spot for water dogs — a wooded peninsula on Lake Austin with swimming access and shaded trails near Tarrytown. Free, unfenced, dogs must have solid recall.

name: Shoal Creek Greenbelt
description:
Shoal Creek Greenbelt runs for miles through central Austin, but only one stretch of it is off-leash: the section between 24th and 29th Streets, a little over a mile end to end. Everywhere else on the greenbelt your dog needs to be leashed, and that boundary is enforced more than people expect given how casual the rest of the trail feels.

What this offers that a fenced run does not is a walk. The off-leash stretch is a corridor, not an enclosure, so dogs move with you rather than orbiting a patch of dirt. For a high-energy dog that has already learned to check in, an out-and-back here does more than an hour in a pen. For a dog that has not, it is the wrong place to find out — there is no fence between the trail and the surrounding streets.

The tree cover is the other draw. This is a genuinely shaded creek bed running below street level through the middle of a dense neighborhood, and in July that shade is worth driving for. The creek gives dogs somewhere to cool off, though it is an urban waterway with the flow to match: after heavy rain it comes up fast and runs dirty, and in a long dry spell it can reduce to standing pools that are not appealing for anyone.

The honest caveat is condition. Shoal Creek has taken repeated flood damage over the years, and sections of trail — including parts of the off-leash stretch — have been closed at various points for erosion repair and construction. It is worth a quick check with Austin Parks and Recreation before making a special trip across town, because a closure here can mean a detour up onto the street rather than a short walk around.

Access is easiest from the residential streets crossing the greenbelt at either end, and parking is on-street in a neighborhood where that is not always simple. Mornings are the better bet, both for spots and for the crowd — this stretch is popular with runners and cyclists as well as dog owners, and a loose dog on a narrow trail meets a lot of traffic at six in the evening.

name: Walnut Creek Metropolitan Park
description:
Walnut Creek is the largest off-leash area in Austin, and the scale changes what a visit actually is. This is 293 acres with roughly fifteen miles of trail running through it, so a trip here is closer to taking your dog on a hike than standing in a fenced run watching them circle. People routinely spend an hour or more and cover real ground.

The off-leash area is north of the creek, which catches first-timers out: the developed side of the park nearer the Lamar entrance — the pool, the ballfields, the playground and picnic areas — is leash-required, and the open running starts once you have crossed over. Signage exists but is not aggressive about it, so you want to know that before you arrive rather than working it out from other people's reactions.

The creek is the main attraction for most dogs. It runs shallow through much of the park with easy gravel entries, and on a summer afternoon there is usually a line of dogs standing in it cooling off. Depth varies a lot with recent rain — most of the year it is ankle to knee deep, but it moves fast after a storm and the limestone underfoot gets slick, so it is not a good day to let a poor swimmer wander in unattended.

The terrain is hilly and wooded, with limestone bluffs and a lot of tree cover, which makes it one of the more tolerable places to be outdoors here in August. It is also genuinely easy to lose track of where you are. The trail network is dense and the junctions look alike, so if your dog ranges wide, keep them in sight rather than trusting they will find you.

One real caution: this is a popular mountain biking park, and the trails are shared. Riders come through at speed, sometimes downhill and quiet, and a dog standing in a blind corner is a problem for everyone. A dog with reliable recall handles this fine. A dog that bolts at movement does not, and weekend mornings are the busiest window for bikes.

Parking is free in the lot off North Lamar and is rarely a problem given the size of the place. There are restrooms near the pool, though not out on the trails, and no water fountains once you are past the developed area — bring your own for a long loop, because the creek is not something you want your dog drinking from after a rain.
metaTitle: Walnut Creek Metropolitan Park (Walnut Creek District Park) — Austin Dog Park Guide
metaDescription: Walnut Creek Metropolitan Park — also called Walnut Creek District Park — has Austin's largest off-leash dog area, 293 acres of trails, and creek access. Hours, rules, and trail map.

name: West Austin Park
description:
West Austin Park takes up a single block in Clarksville, and the off-leash area is a fenced section of it rather than the whole park. That distinction matters here more than at most places. Friends of West Austin Park, the volunteer group that helps look after the grounds, asks plainly that dogs stay leashed everywhere outside the fence, and the reasoning is practical rather than fussy: the open field runs right up against the playground and the pool, and an unfamiliar dog jogging toward someone's kid unsettles people no matter how friendly it is.

Inside the fence it is a compact, heavily used run with water and waste bags on site. Most evenings bring the same faces, which is the real character of the place — a neighborhood park in the older sense, where people know each other's dogs by name and notice a new one.

The rest of the block is worth knowing about if kids are coming along. The wading pool runs roughly 1 to 8pm for stretches of June through August, stays under four feet throughout, and has a lifeguard on duty. Restrooms are inside the 1930s Tudor-style bathhouse beside it. There is a playscape, a basketball hoop, a swing set tucked behind the pool, and picnic tables that cannot be reserved, birthday party or not.

Parking is on the street in a dense neighborhood, so mornings are considerably easier than evenings.
features: Separate areas for large and small dogs
metaTitle: West Austin Park Dog Park | Fenced Off-Leash Area in Clarksville
metaDescription: Fenced off-leash area at West Austin Park in Clarksville. Dogs must stay leashed elsewhere in the park. Wading pool, playscape and 1930s bathhouse on site. Free, open 5am-10pm daily.

name: Zilker Metropolitan Park
leashPolicy: On-Leash except the Great Lawn (off-leash, unfenced)
description:
Zilker is Austin's front lawn — 351 acres of open ground between Barton Springs Road and Lady Bird Lake — and the part that matters for dogs is more specific than most people realize.

**The off-leash area is the Great Lawn.** Everywhere else in Zilker, dogs are required to be leashed, including the paths, the picnic areas and the ground around Barton Springs Pool. The Great Lawn is not fenced, and it sits in the middle of one of the busiest parks in the city, so this is somewhere for a dog with genuinely reliable recall rather than a place to practice it. On a Saturday there will be frisbee games, picnics, small children and someone's off-duty band all happening within a hundred yards.

Timing is most of the experience here. Early on a weekday the lawn is close to empty and it is one of the best places in Austin to let a dog stretch out. Weekend afternoons, or anything during a festival build-out, it is chaos — and the park periodically closes sections entirely for event setup, which is worth checking if you are making a special trip.

Barton Creek runs along the southern edge with natural wading access, and the hike-and-bike trail along Lady Bird Lake connects from the north side, both on leash.

A water caution that applies here: Austin Parks and Recreation warns that toxic algae has been found in Lady Bird Lake and is most likely present in summer and autumn. It can be fatal to dogs, which are exposed by drinking and by licking it off their coat afterwards. Keep dogs away from floating mats and scummy still water at the edges, and rinse them with clean water when you leave.

Parking is the other constraint. The lots off Barton Springs Road and Stratford Drive fill early at weekends and cost money most of the year; street parking nearby is limited and enforced.
features: Connects to Lady Bird Lake hike-and-bike trail
metaTitle: Zilker Metropolitan Park Austin — Dog-Friendly Trails & Barton Creek Access | ATX Dog Parks
metaDescription: Dogs welcome at Zilker Metropolitan Park — 351 acres of open greenspace near Barton Springs and Lady Bird Lake in central Austin. On-leash required. Best for morning walks and creek access.
